claims.text: The initial Fe–Co–Ni–Mn–Cr alloy with minor Al additions is primarily single-phase and has a homogeneous as-cast microstructure.
Annealing at 700°C for 1–6 hours followed by rapid quenching will induce nanoscale precipitates in the alloy.
The annealing-induced nanoscale precipitates will be dispersed within a primarily single-phase matrix.
The nanoscale precipitates generate localized internal stress fields.
Precipitate-induced local stress fields modulate magnetic exchange interactions.
Modulation of magnetic exchange interactions reduces the applied magnetic field required to initiate a magnetocaloric phase transition.
Connectivity of the matrix maintains rapid thermal conduction.
Connectivity of the matrix preserves mechanical stability after precipitation.
A refined precipitate distribution mitigates magnetic hysteresis by promoting uniform magnetic-domain switching.
An optimally sized and well-distributed precipitate population will enhance the magnetocaloric effect at lower applied fields relative to the as-cast baseline.
An optimally sized and well-distributed precipitate population will reduce magnetic hysteresis relative to the as-cast baseline.
Annealed samples with an optimal precipitate population will have mechanical properties comparable to or better than the as-cast baseline.
Excessive annealing can produce precipitates that are too large or inhomogeneously distributed.
Coarse or inhomogeneously distributed precipitates can degrade the beneficial modulation of magnetic exchange interactions.
Coarse or inhomogeneously distributed precipitates can degrade magnetocaloric performance.
Coarse or inhomogeneously distributed precipitates can degrade mechanical performance.
Variations in minor alloying elements and processing conditions can alter the coupling between microstructure and magnetic properties.
